name: side channel river Waal Hurwenen Zaltbommel Netherlands 338 pm  260802_0149
description:
A summery and windy day by the side channel and ‘Kil van Hurwenen’ nature reserve, on the River Waal near Zaltbommel in the Netherlands. Many birds like Gulls and Terns in front. The humming of passing ships over the river on 500 metre.
About the picture From the bank, you look out over a tranquil stretch of water, a wide tributary of the river. The water is still and reflects the blue sky dotted with soft, white clouds. To the left lies a natural, somewhat untidy bank of sand and mud, where the branches of overhanging trees almost touch the water. On that left bank lies an old shipwreck. It has partly sunk into the sand and is clearly weathered by time and water. The wreck lies still and abandoned, a striking yet peaceful feature of the landscape. On the right-hand side, you can see a strip of land with dense vegetation: trees, bushes and grass running along the riverbank. Behind that strip lies another stretch of water, giving the landscape the appearance of a green embrace around the channel. In the distance, at the far left, lies the wide River Waal. You can recognise it by its open water surface, the wide horizon and the inland vessel just passing by.

About the shipwreck The wreck has been lying in the Kil since 1978, but possibly even earlier. The shipwreck in the Kil at Hurwenen is a steel ‘hevelaak’ (Hagenaar) named Henrica Maria. The ship, built for freight transport, had a hold with a fore and aft section and measures over 21 by 4 metres. The ship was equipped with a mast and boom with a unloading mechanism, as well as a side-thruster system powered by a diesel engine, but none of these components remain.
About the The Kil van Hurwenen The Kil van Hurwenen (also known as the Hurwenensche Uiterwaarden) is a nature reserve covering approximately 146 hectares in the floodplain of the Waal near the village of Hurwenen (municipality of Maasdriel). The area is still regularly flooded at high water and was formed when an old meander of the Waal was cut off from the river in 1639. In order to improve the river’s course, this bend in the Waal was cut off in 1639, leaving the Kil as a cut-off river branch. This was done by the river administrator of the time, who wanted to straighten the course of the Waal. For centuries, the area was used for haymaking and as pasture for livestock. In the 19th century, clay was extracted there for the brickworks. During high water, the area is still flooded with river water; work has also been carried out to improve the quality of the natural environment and water, including the construction of a parallel channel that flows alongside the main channel. The word ‘kil’ in ‘Kil van Hurwenen’ is Old Dutch for a water channel or stream carved out by flowing water.

name: polder birds hot-air balloon Lage Zwaluwe Netherlands 905 am 251012_0049
description:
Early, windless Sunday morning in the Nieuwe Zwaluwsche Polder, on the northern edge of Lage Zwaluwe in the Netherlands. The greylag geese fly overhead in flocks. A common sandpiper, a crow, and a curlew. Above them—just vanished into the low-hanging clouds—the sound of a hot air balloon intermittently opening its burner. What brings me joy is the repeated call of the kestrel.
Description of the photo of the Nieuwe Zwaluwsche Polder: The photo shows a vast polder landscape beneath a heavily overcast sky. The fields are a fresh green and subtly vary in color. In the distance, rows of trees line the edge of the river Amer, and scattered throughout are a few farms and rural homes. The sky is mostly grey and closed, but on the horizon there's a small break in the cloud cover, where a soft glow of sunlight shines through. That light gives the landscape a serene, almost motionless atmosphere.

It is a historic polder that was established around 1650. It lies within a region that is part of a system of polders and creeks formed after flooding events and subsequently reclaimed and managed. The polder is one of the smaller ones in this area and was created to obtain fertile agricultural land. The long dikes of the polder were initially difficult to protect against the sea, and over time, measures were taken to adapt the water system and improve its defenses. The area involved plays an important role in both agriculture and nature development, with a mix of natural habitats such as reed marshes and flower-rich grasslands alongside farmland. The polder is a historic and recognizable landscape in the Netherlands, with a rich legacy of land reclamation, water management, and agricultural development.
